_note: Sensitosis Normie test bank: everyday detectors, no medicine. Same format as tests.json, plus yes/no (plural nouns for cases with and without the thing), all (plural noun for everything), pos/neg (verbs for flagged/cleared). kind: gadget | software | animal | human | check. sens = catches it when it's there; spec = stays quiet when it isn't. v = figure used for the reveal; lo/hi = range that scores full marks. spec null = sensitivity-only round. Every figure was read from the linked page, checked 2 Nov 2026.

aidet.scenario: A teacher feeds a stack of essays into the free AI-text classifier OpenAI released in January 2023.
aidet.says: It caught about 1 in 4 AI texts and wrongly accused about 1 in 11 human ones. OpenAI switched it off six months later for its ‘low rate of accuracy’. Points for honesty.
aidet.note: OpenAI’s own challenge set of English texts. Retired on 20 July 2023.
src: OpenAI: New AI classifier for indicating AI-written text (2023)

turnitin.test: Turnitin AI-writing detector (the company’s own figures)
turnitin.scenario: A uni assignment goes through Turnitin, which now gives an ‘AI-written’ percentage alongside the plagiarism check.
turnitin.says: On paper, miles better than OpenAI’s effort: it says it may miss up to 15% of AI text and wrongly flags under 1% of fully human work. Those are the company’s own numbers, not an independent test, and it says not to use the score alone.
turnitin.note: Turnitin’s published claims, as reported by Purdue University (2024). It only flags text when it is ‘98% sure’.
src: Purdue University: Turnitin adding AI writing detection, but use it with caution (2024)

fingerprint.test: Fingerprint expert matching a crime-scene print
fingerprint.scenario: A smudgy print lifted from a crime scene is compared with a known print by a trained examiner.
fingerprint.says: Wrong matches were very rare, about 1 in 1,000. Missed matches were far more common, about 1 in 13, and 85% of examiners missed at least one. Having a second examiner recheck caught all the wrong matches.
fingerprint.note: The FBI-backed ‘black box’ study (Ulery 2011, PNAS): 169 examiners, about 100 print pairs each.
src: Phys.org: False positives rare from fingerprint examiners (2011)

bedfield.test: Bed bug sniffer dog, in real apartments
bedfield.scenario: A trained beagle and handler sweep through apartments with real, natural infestations.
bedfield.says: In the real world the dogs found under half the bugs, and false alarms averaged 15%. Teams ranged from finding 10% to 100%, so it’s about the handler as much as the nose.
bedfield.note: Cooper, Wang and Singh 2014, Journal of Economic Entomology: 11 dog teams in naturally infested apartments.
src: Cooper et al. 2014: Accuracy of trained canines for detecting bed bugs (Rutgers PDF)

bedlab.test: Bed bug sniffer dog, in a set-up test room
bedlab.scenario: Researchers hide bed bugs in hotel rooms, then send in a trained dog to find them.
bedlab.says: Exam conditions, top marks: 98% found, zero false alarms. Then the same kind of dogs went into real apartments. See the other version. Practice is not the match.
bedlab.note: Pfiester 2008 controlled hotel-room hides, as reported in Cooper et al. 2014.
src: Cooper et al. 2014: Accuracy of trained canines for detecting bed bugs (Rutgers PDF)

polygraph.scenario: A suspect is wired up. Breathing, sweat and blood pressure are tracked while an examiner asks questions.
polygraph.says: Better than a coin toss, worse than its TV reputation. Roughly 1 in 5 honest people fail. In the US National Academies’ spy-screening example, a test that was 99.5% ‘correct’ overall still let 8 of 10 spies through.
polygraph.note: US National Research Council review (2003). A US Defense polygraph study gave about 85% and 78%; across lab studies, the catch rate ranged widely depending on how many false alarms you accept (10–30%).
src: National Academies: The Polygraph and Lie Detection (2003), chapter 5

humanlie.scenario: Someone tells you a story. You watch their face, listen to their voice and decide: lie or truth?
humanlie.says: Across more than 24,000 people in over 200 studies, we caught under half the lies, and got 54% right overall. Slightly better than a coin. We lean towards believing people, which is nice, if not great detective work.
humanlie.note: Bond and DePaulo 2006 meta-analysis, Personality and Social Psychology Review: 24,483 judges.
src: Bond and DePaulo 2006: Accuracy of deception judgments (PDF)

lineupsim.test: Police line-up, all faces at once
lineupsim.scenario: A witness looks at six faces side by side. Sometimes the culprit is there, sometimes not.
lineupsim.says: With the culprit there, witnesses picked them about half the time. With the culprit absent, most still picked someone. Memory badly wants to help, even when it can’t.
lineupsim.note: Steblay, Dysart and Wells 2011 meta-analysis of 72 lab tests. ‘Stays quiet’ means the witness says the culprit isn’t there.
src: Steblay, Dysart and Wells 2011: line-up meta-analysis (PDF)

lineupseq.test: Police line-up, one face at a time
lineupseq.scenario: Same witness, new method: faces are shown one by one, with a yes or no for each.
lineupseq.says: One at a time catches fewer culprits but makes far fewer wrong picks when the culprit isn’t there. A trade-off, not a free lunch.
lineupseq.note: Steblay, Dysart and Wells 2011 meta-analysis: 72 tests overall, 27 in the strictest subset.
src: Steblay, Dysart and Wells 2011: line-up meta-analysis (PDF)

tsa.condition: a smuggled weapon or fake bomb
tsa.scenario: 2015: undercover government ‘red teams’ pose as passengers and try to sneak banned items through US airport checkpoints.
tsa.says: The checkpoints stopped 3 of 70. That’s a 95% fail rate. Your water bottle never stood a chance, though.
tsa.note: US Homeland Security covert tests, confirmed by a government official in June 2015.
src: Fox13 / CNN: TSA screeners failed 67 of 70 undercover tests (2015)

captcha.scenario: A website makes you type squiggly letters to prove you’re not a robot.
captcha.says: Bots solved these almost every time, in under a second. Humans got 50 to 84% right and took up to 15 seconds. So the robot test mostly blocks… people.
captcha.note: Searles et al. 2023, ‘An Empirical Study and Evaluation of Modern CAPTCHAs’: 1,400 people. Bot accuracy was ‘just under 100%’, so anything from 0 to 5 scores full marks.
src: TechXplore: Bots are better at CAPTCHA than humans (2023)

pas.scenario: Night-time traffic stop. The officer chats through the window holding a torch with a built-in alcohol sensor. No blowing required.
pas.says: Catches about 3 in 4 drivers over the US 0.08 limit just from their breath in the air, and almost never flags a sober driver. Plot twist: in this study, handing out the torches didn’t change the arrest rate at all.
pas.note: Field figures (6 of 9 bars) cited in Fell, Compton and Voas 2008, Traffic Injury Prevention. Australia’s usual limit is lower, 0.05.
src: Fell, Compton and Voas 2008: passive alcohol sensors at traffic stops (PMC)

facerec.scenario: London: a camera on a police van scans faces in a busy street and checks them against a watchlist.
facerec.says: Catches about 9 in 10 people on the list and wrongly flags about 1 in 6,000 passers-by. Tiny, until 60,000 people walk past. At looser settings than the default, false alarms weren’t shared equally: Black faces were wrongly flagged more often.
facerec.note: UK National Physical Laboratory testing for the Met and South Wales Police (2023), at the default 0.6 setting.
src: The Register: UK police facial recognition test results (2023)

smoke.test: Home smoke alarm in a real fire
smoke.scenario: A fire breaks out at home, big enough to set off an alarm. There’s an alarm on the ceiling. Does it go off?
smoke.says: It went off in 88% of fires. But in fires where someone died and an alarm was present, it sounded only 71% of the time. And for the record: 73% of people said the last time theirs went off, it was cooking.
smoke.note: US National Fire Protection Association report (Jan 2019), 2012–2016 home fires. No good figure for false alarms, so one slider today.
src: NFPA: Smoke Alarms in US Home Fires (2019, PDF)

bombdog.scenario: 56 dog-and-handler teams search test areas with hidden explosives. These figures are for the top eight.
bombdog.says: Even the best teams found about 8 in 10, short of the official 90% standard. None of the 56 teams met it. Very good dogs, very tough exam.
bombdog.note: DeGreeff, Prada-Tiedemann et al. 2025, Frontiers in Veterinary Science. The standard asks for 90% found and under 10% false alerts.
src: Frontiers news: explosive detection dogs assessment (2025)
